overview: This file assembles U.S. diplomatic, intelligence, and broadcast-monitoring records on Japanese-controlled railways and wartime transportation from 1941 to 1944, with one later routing leaf from 1945. It covers a newly opened line between Wonsan and Pyongyang; railway personnel, training, rolling stock, traffic, and military carrying capacity in Korea and Manchuria; Japan’s projected Tokyo–Shimonoseki high-speed “bullet express”; the opening of the Kanmon undersea tunnel; railway-loading and employment indices; and restrictions on passenger travel imposed to release personnel for evacuation transport. The bundle combines FBI correspondence, State Department cross-references and routing sheets, a substantial War Department intelligence report with photographs, diplomatic despatches and telegrams, a translated press article, and monitored broadcasts, including several items on French Indochina that are only incidentally related to the railway subject.

subfiles.title: Hoover letter on the Wonsan–Pyongyang railway
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports confidential information that a new railway between Wonsan on the Sea of Japan and Pyongyang in northern Korea had entered service.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards intelligence on a new Japanese-occupied Korea railway to naval and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on Japanese industries and railways
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to the original memorandum concerning Japanese industries and railways in State Department file 894.60/24.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a 1941 memo on Japanese industries and railways drew on a confidential outside source.

subfiles.title: State Department routing sheet for Manchuria and Korea railway report
subfiles.from: Department of State, Under Secretary’s Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Records the internal circulation and filing of the military intelligence report on railways in Manchuria and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Routing sheet circulates 1942 intelligence on Manchuria and Korea railways across State Department offices.

subfiles.title: Military intelligence report on railway transportation in Manchuria and Korea
subfiles.doc_type: military intelligence report with photographic enclosures
subfiles.from: New York Office, Military Intelligence Service; report prepared by John L. Curtis
subfiles.about: Assesses railway personnel, training, equipment, traffic, control systems, and military carrying capacity in Manchuria and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on Fred Thomas, Japanese and Manchukuo yearbooks, and Japanese government railway reports, this study estimates staffing and rolling stock for the Chosen State Lines, South Manchurian Railway, and Manchukuo State Lines. It describes training institutes at Dalian, Shenyang, Harbin, Jilin, and Qiqihar; American-influenced rolling-stock standards; the streamlined ASIA locomotive and train; troop capacities; repair facilities; freight and passenger volumes; seasonal traffic; and signalling methods. The attached photographs show soybean loading at Jilin, training at the Shenyang Railway Training Institute, and a streamlined locomotive produced at the railway workshops.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on the Tokyo–Shimonoseki high-speed line
subfiles.from: H. P., Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Comments on the Buenos Aires despatch concerning construction of Japan’s projected high-speed trunk railway.
subfiles.summary: Memo notes Japan's long-discussed Tokyo-Shimonoseki high-speed line would follow the existing Tokaido route.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires despatch on work begun for the Japanese bullet railway
subfiles.from: Richard Fors, First Secretary of Embassy, for the U.S. Ambassador in Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese-language press claims that construction had begun on a 989-kilometre high-speed railway between Tokyo and Shimonoseki.
subfiles.summary: Buenos Aires relays Japanese press reports on bullet-train construction plans, suggesting US air reconnaissance note the work.

subfiles.title: Translation of Domei article on the Tokyo–Shimonoseki bullet express
subfiles.from: Domei; translated from Diario Nan-A by the U.S. Embassy in Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: Department of State, as enclosure to despatch no. 8108
subfiles.about: Provides detailed plans for the proposed 989-kilometre standard-gauge bullet-express route and its tunnels, stations, bridges, and projected speeds.
subfiles.summary: Translation: Japan's Shimonoseki bullet-train tunneling work is accelerating in 1943, targeting 100-200 km/h speeds though completion remains a decade off.

subfiles.title: Bern telegram on Japanese government railway loadings
subfiles.from: Leland B. Harrison, U.S. Legation, Bern
subfiles.about: Transmits official Japanese index figures showing increased government railway loadings in early 1943.
subfiles.summary: Bern reports Japanese government railway loadings rose in early 1943 compared with the prior year.

subfiles.title: Bern telegram on Japanese factory and mining employment indices
subfiles.from: Leland B. Harrison, U.S. Legation, Bern
subfiles.about: Supplements the railway-loading telegram with Japanese factory and mining employment indices through February 1943.
subfiles.summary: Bern relays Japanese factory and mining employment indices showing substantial wartime growth through early 1943.

subfiles.title: Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service reports on the Kanmon Tunnel and Indochina
subfiles.from: Department of State, drawing on Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service reports
subfiles.about: Summarizes broadcasts on the opening of the Kanmon railway tunnel and on political conditions in French Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Broadcast intelligence reports the Kanmon rail tunnel's 1942 opening cutting Tokyo-Kagoshima travel time, plus unrelated Indochina items.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram on restrictions on passenger traffic in Japan
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, U.S. Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Relays a Soviet press report that Japan would restrict passenger rail travel from April 1, 1944.
subfiles.summary: Moscow relays Izvestiya's report that Japan is restricting passenger rail travel and reassigning staff to evacuation transport.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs routing note concerning an Embassy enclosure
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Directs attention to the penultimate paragraph of an unidentified Embassy enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary routing note flags an unidentified enclosure's key paragraph for special attention.

interest: Shows wartime US tracking of Japan's railway system, from a proposed bullet train to intensifying wartime transport strain.
